extracted.intended_audience: general readers and practitioners interested in 19th-century automata construction, stage magic, and mechanical craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical criteria for designing, building, testing, and exhibiting mechanical automata and related stage-illusion techniques (heads, bird-song imitations, silent mechanisms, card-marking tricks, and showmanship). Draws on 19th‑century artisan/magician practice and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automaton head: expression must match character
rubrics_metrics.description: The automaton's head must convey the intelligent expression appropriate to the character (e.g., a writer in Louis XV costume should not wear a 'Christ' head).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author recounts commissioning multiple sculptors: one produced a Christ-like head (anachronistic), another a featureless Nuremberg mannequin head; both were inappropriate. The author modeled and carved a head himself (ultimately making a self‑resemblance) as the correct solution. Anti-pattern: accepting a technically fine sculpture that is thematically wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct models and iterative self-study
rubrics_metrics.description: When no suitable model exists, study oneself (mirror front and profile) and iteratively shape the model until the desired expression is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author describes posing 'in posture d'écrivain', feeling forms, repeatedly cutting and adding until eyes, mouth, nose acquired the intended human appearance. Emphasizes hands‑on, iterative touch/retouch process leading to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act immediately on conceived projects (persistence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin execution of a project as soon as it is conceived and persist despite difficulties ('vouloir c'est pouvoir').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author characterizes himself as tenacious: upon conception he immediately set to work despite prior failures with sculptors, and this temperament produced results. Guidance is motivational: persistence coupled with hands-on work yields success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for mechanical simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the mechanism to be as simple as possible while achieving the required functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author deliberately reduced parts and sought simple, efficient solutions (akin to nature's complex but imperceptible instruments). He cites efforts to simplify his writer automaton and his satisfaction at minimal, elegant mechanisms. Warning: later audience perceptions may reward apparent complexity (see next criterion), but artistic correctness favors simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer imperceptible (silent) operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make mechanisms run without audible noise—operate imperceptibly to better imitate natural effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author spent great effort to eliminate noise in the writer automaton's gears to imitate nature. Example of good practice: conceal harmony of parts so the mechanism does not betray itself. Anti-pattern: allowing audible gear noise that reveals artifice (though see trade-off below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware audience equates visible/audible complexity with merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Public often judges mechanical merit by the multiplicity of visible parts or by audible commotion; greater apparent complexity often increases popular admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes that the lay public appreciates 'multiplicity des pièces' and louder mechanical sounds (tohu‑bohu). He experimented by reintroducing clatter to increase popular acclaim, but later judged that choice mistaken (returned to quiet, simpler mechanism). Use this knowledge strategically but ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice artistic rules to produce spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'overcharging' or exaggerating mechanical or theatrical elements merely to produce a greater immediate effect; such excess departs from the rules of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to actors who 'chargent leurs rôles' to win laughs—successful for crowd-pleasing but not for true artistry. Author considered his addition of mechanical noise a mistake and restored the original restrained design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze natural phenomena into representable mechanical parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: To imitate complex natural phenomena (e.g., the nightingale's song), decompose sounds into analyzable components (tones, semitones, pauses, modulations) and map them to mechanical parameters (e.g., degrees of a circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author developed a 'méthode moitié musicale, moitié mécanique' using numbers tied to circle degrees to represent musical elements. He used a tiny copper tube and piston as the 'gosier' and a clockwork to drive a bellows and valves to reproduce articulations and modulations. Practical guidance: reduce musical subtleties to discrete, controllable mechanical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical field study and iterative tuning
rubrics_metrics.description: Train by listening to live models (e.g., the nightingale in woods), compare, and iteratively correct the mechanism until imitation is satisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author spent nights in the Bois de Romainville to isolate a principal singer, copied phrases, then repeatedly adjusted the machine across multiple visits until he achieved the intended result. Practical method: observe in-situ, transcribe/imitate, implement mechanical corrections, retest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design coordinated motion and sound (synchronization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Animate visible parts (beak, wings, hops, head turns) in coordination with the produced sounds to create a convincing imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author required the bird's beak to move with articulated sounds, wings to beat, and jumps between branches in sync with musical output. This necessitates mechanical linkages timed by the same drive that controls the vocal piston and valves.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-test protocol: staged initial trials with trusted lay observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct first public demonstrations with trusted household/casual observers (e.g., portière and her husband) to gauge reactions and collect feedback before wider exhibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asked his porter's family to attend first trials; anecdotes illustrate how lay comments (often naive) can be amusing and sometimes generate ideas but should not dictate technical design. Testing included asking simple programmed questions (e.g., 'Quel est l’artiste qui t’a donné l’être?') and checking practical functions (writing signature, telling time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage and filter lay criticism and unsolicited suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect simplistic, irrelevant, or misguided suggestions from non‑specialists; appreciate good intent but retain expert judgment when deciding changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the porter suggested replacing a levrette drawing by a caniche and adding an entire scene (blind man, child) which would obscure the emblem; the porter then proposed labeling the desired emblem to 'clarify' it. Author found such remarks comic and did not adopt them. Use lay feedback selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestidigitation business technique: feign wealth to elicit generosity from pupils ('pigeon' method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method used to extract higher payment from students/clients: pretend to be wealthy during demonstration, display/feign coins (drop/produce them), leave a few visible, prompting the pupil to increase the offered payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed procedure given: allow pupil to set the lesson price, feign accidentally producing and then casually collecting gold pieces, but intentionally leave some visible on the table to suggest abundance; the pupil typically reciprocates by adding money. Ethics: this is a described trick of doubtful morality (author recounts as confessions of a professional 'Grec').

rubrics_metrics.name: Card-marking scheme: single-point grid encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: A single small matte point placed at a specific intersection on a divided grid of the card can encode both rank and suit, making every card identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains dividing the card visually into eight vertical by four horizontal zones; the intersection where a tiny point is placed indicates the card's value and color/suit. He discovered such marks appearing to disappear/reappear with viewing angle. Practical caution: knowledge of the scheme can detect cheating but can also be misused; author initially hesitates to disclose it but then explains to inform readers for protection ('pour éviter un danger, il faut le connaître').

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert examination technique for suspected altered cards
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically inspect suspicious card decks with good lighting and magnification, examining backs and angles for imperceptible marks that may appear/disappear with viewing distance or tilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author spent fifteen days nightly examining 150 decks with his eyes and a loupe, looking for imperceptible matte points; he notes the phenomenon of a point visible only at certain distances/angles. Practical procedure: methodical, patient inspection; vary viewing distance and illumination.
